catalog_quote: In Papuan Malay, primary stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the lexical root, while secondary stress is assigned to the alternating syllable preceding the one carrying the primary stress. These stress patterns apply to lexical roots (§2.4.4.1) as well as to lexical items that are historically derived by (unproductive) affixation (§2.4.4.2). ... Most disyllabic roots have penultimate stress (900/1,004 items – 90%), as illustrated in Table 2.39. The remaining 104 items (10%) have ultimate stress and display the following pattern. In 101 of the 104 roots (97%), the unstressed penultimate syllable contains the front open-near vowel /ɛ/. ... Front open-near /ɛ/, however, does not condition ultimate stress, as in 61 of the 900 lexical roots with penultimate stress (7%) the stressed syllable also contains front /ɛ/. ... The data presented in Table 2.39 to Table 2.41 demonstr…
sweep_summary: Papuan Malay is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed (penultimate primary stress of the root, secondary on alternating preceding syllables; ~10% roots with ultimate stress, 97% of them with /ɛ/ in the penult), deciding source Kluge 2017 (open-access reference grammar, sect. 2.4.4, pp. 96-99). The 8 stress/prosody-titled items are all Kaland/Himmelmann-circle work from 2018-2020. Read in full: Kaland, Himmelmann & Kluge 2019 ICPhS (downloaded; first-hand random-forest analysis of Kluge's corpus: penult 932 / ult 108; ultimate stress only when the penult has /ε/ and the final syllable has no mid vowel — refines the exception statement), Riesberg et al. 2020 Lab. Phonology (downloaded by automated download default UA past the Anubis bot-check; restates Kluge's 90/10 distribution, calls the acoustic support 'some, though not particularly strong', and concludes PM listeners barely agree on prominences — a caution on the status of 'lexical stress', not on position), plus the already-held Kaland 2018 SP (spectral tilt confirms Kluge), Riesberg et al. 2018 (same caution, p. 407) and Kaland, Bracks & Himmelmann 2018 (silent). Abstract-only: Kaland & Baumann 2020 JASA and Kaland & Himmelmann 2020 Lang. & Speech (both phrase-level/discourse prosody, silent on placement). Still unread: Kaland 2019 J. Phonetics (the flagship acoustic confirmation; hybrid-OA but ScienceDirect/Elsevier API could not be reached by automated download, and the author-hosted copies on sfb1252.uni-koeln.de listed in Kaland's CV are unreachable because every uni-koeln.de host refuses connections by automated download; the Internet Archive was offline) and Kaland, Kluge & van Heuven 2021 Phonetica (same host). Net: coding confirmed and refined; no source supersedes Kluge 2017; suggested edits are an evidence-grade upgrade citing Kaland et al. 2019 ICPhS / Kaland 2018 / Kaland 2019 as instrumental confirmation, the sharper exception rule, and a caution line for the Riesberg et al. 'stressless Malayic' position.

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Papuan Malay occurs mostly on the penultimate syllable, except when this syllable contains /ε/ [11]. For example, in /tε.ˈkan/ ('to press') stress moves to /kan/ because /ε/ could reduce to schwa, which cannot be stressed. Thus, in /ˈtu.kan/ ('craftsman') stress occurs on the default penultimate syllable. [...] ultimate stress is mainly found when /ε/ occurred in the first syllable, confirming [11]. [...] When the penult contains /ε/, stress shifts to the ultimate syllable only when the ultimate does not contain a mid-vowel.
new_statements.citation: Kaland, Constantijn, Nikolaus P. Himmelmann & Angela Kluge. 2019. Stress predictors in a Papuan Malay random forest. Proceedings of the 19th ICPhS (Melbourne), 2871-2875.
new_statements.locator: sect. 1, p. 2871 (rule); sect. 3 and Table 3, pp. 2873-2874 (criteria and counts: penult 932, ult 108)
new_statements.reading: First-hand corpus analysis (with the grammar's author) of the same 1,040-root word list underlying Kluge 2017: primary stress is penultimate by default (932/1,040, 90%); the 108 ultimate-stress roots are those with /ε/ in the penult whose final syllable lacks a mid vowel, leaving 33 residual exceptions (<4%). This is a fixed-penultimate system with a lexically restricted, vowel-conditioned shift to the final syllable — the same coding the catalog holds, with a sharper statement of the exception condition. Complemented by Kaland 2018 (spectral tilt) and, as reported in Kaland 2021 pp. 9-10 and Riesberg et al. 2020 p. 3, Kaland 2019 (duration, vowel quality, tilt), which acoustically confirm Kluge's stressed/unstressed distinction; Riesberg et al. 2018/2020 add the caution that native listeners do not perceive this as a prominence distinction.

sources.citation: Kaland, Constantijn, Nikolaus P. Himmelmann & Angela Kluge. 2019. Stress predictors in a Papuan Malay random forest. In Calhoun, Escudero, Tabain & Warren (eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (Melbourne), 2871-2875. [Glottolog 572584; already listed]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.quote: p. 2871: 'Word stress in Papuan Malay occurs mostly on the penultimate syllable, except when this syllable contains /ε/ [11]. For example, in /tε.ˈkan/ ("to press") stress moves to /kan/ because /ε/ could reduce to schwa, which cannot be stressed. Thus, in /ˈtu.kan/ ("craftsman") stress occurs on the default penultimate syllable.' pp. 2873-2874: 'ultimate stress is mainly found when /ε/ occurred in the first syllable, confirming [11]. ... When the penult contains /ε/, stress shifts to the ultimate syllable only when the ultimate does not contain a mid-vowel.' Table 3: Total penult 932, ult 108.
sources.locator: sect. 1, p. 2871; sect. 3 and Table 3, pp. 2873-2874
sources.note: First-hand lexical (random-forest) analysis of Kluge's 1,040-word corpus with Kluge as co-author: penultimate by default (932/1,040 = 90%); ultimate stress (108) almost always when the penult has /ε/ AND the final syllable lacks a mid vowel; /a/ in the final syllable weakly attracts stress; 25 penult-stress and 8 ult-stress residual exceptions (<4%). Refines the catalog's exception statement (adds the final-syllable mid-vowel condition) without changing the penultimate coding.

sources.citation: Riesberg, Sonja, Janina Kalbertodt, Stefan Baumann & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann. 2020. Using Rapid Prosody Transcription to probe little-known prosodic systems: The case of Papuan Malay. Laboratory Phonology 11(1): 8, 1-35. doi:10.5334/labphon.192 [Glottolog 671707; not previously listed]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 3: 'This is also the analysis proposed for PM by Kluge (2017). ... Kluge concludes that 964 (90%) of all words have penultimate stress ... and only 108 (10%) have stress on the final syllable. Of the 108 words that displayed ultimate stress, 105 (97%) contained the front open-mid vowel /ɛ/ ... in the penultimate syllable. Yet, Kluge notes that /ɛ/ does not condition ultimate stress ... Importantly, Kluge's analysis is exclusively based on her own auditory judgment'. p. 1: perception experiments 'support the claim made in earlier (production) studies that Malayic varieties appear to lack stress (i.e., lexical stress as well as post-lexical pitch accents).'
sources.locator: abstract p. 1; sect. 2.1, p. 3; sect. 6 'Conclusion', p. 32
sources.note: Extended RPT study (PM and German listeners). Restates Kluge's penultimate-default distribution and the /ɛ/ exceptions as the standing description, notes it rests on auditory judgment with 'some, though not particularly strong' acoustic support from Kaland 2019, and concludes (p. 32) that PM listeners 'show very little agreement on prosodic prominences when judging excerpts from their native language' — i.e. PM may lack lexical stress as a perceived category. Refines; a caution line for the record, no change to position.

sources.citation: Kaland, Constantijn. 2018. Spectral tilt as a correlate of Papuan Malay word stress. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2018 (Poznań), 339-343. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2018-69 [Glottolog 573231; already listed]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'All values reported show evidence for shallower spectral tilt in syllables that were claimed to be stressed compared to syllables claimed to be unstressed. These findings essentially confirm earlier reports of word stress in Papuan Malay ([4] = Kluge 2017, [11]), unlike the case of Ambonese Malay.'
sources.note: Spectral-tilt measurements on 3,431 penult-stressed vs 198 ult-stressed syllables show shallower tilt in the syllables Kluge marks as stressed; explicitly confirms Kluge 2017 ([4]). Adds the caveat that if PM has word stress 'it is unlikely to be phonemic [4]'.

In Riesberg, Shiohara & Utsumi (eds.), Perspectives on information structure in Austronesian languages (SDL 21), 389-414. Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.1402559 [Glottolog 596749; already listed]

sources.quote: p. 408: 'the current study supports the conclusions of earlier studies that lexical stress is not part of the prosodic system of Malayic varieties. ... the cases of Papuan and Ambon Malay are particularly interesting in this regard, because pitch modulations here appear to be ... very regular and clearly anchored to different syllables (penultimate or final) ... this distinction does not appear to be perceived as a prominence distinction by native speakers.' A Rapid Prosody Transcription (perception) study; it does not dispute WHERE the regular prominence falls (penultimate/final) but whether
sources.locator: sect. 1 pp. 391-392 (summary of Kluge 2014: 964/1,072 = 90% penultimate); conclusion p. 408
sources.note: Rapid Prosody Transcription perception study. Accepts Kluge's 90% penultimate / 10% final distribution as the description of where the regular prominence sits, but argues that native listeners do not perceive it as a prominence distinction, so 'lexical stress' in the standard sense may not exist in Malayic varieties. Refines (a caution on the status of stress), does not contradict the penultimate coding.

sources.quote: The current study investigates the extent to which Papuan Malay phrase prosody is used for demarcating and highlighting, taking into account the potential influence of word stress. This is done by means of acoustic analyses on a corpus of spontaneous speech. Both the form (F0 movement) and the possible functions (demarcating and highlighting) of the final two syllables in Papuan Malay phrases are investigated. Although most results favor the demarcating function of Papuan Malay phrase prosody, a highlighting function cannot be ruled out.
sources.note: Phrase-level F0 study; the abstract says nothing about where word stress falls. Its ICPhS 2019 precursor (Kaland & Baumann 2019, downloaded, see extra item) treats stress position as given ('the frequent occurrence of penultimate stress') and finds F0 movements do not correlate with word stress.

sources.quote: The current study investigates to what extent repetition reduction occurs in Papuan Malay ... An acoustic analysis is carried out on repeated words in short stories produced by native Papuan Malay speakers. The results show that upon repetition, words were shortened and produced with higher F0. In a subsequent word identification task, it was found that first and second mentions were equally intelligible.
sources.note: Discourse-level reduction of repeated words (duration, F0); nothing on word-stress position. Its Speech Prosody 2018 precursor (held by the project) is likewise silent on stress placement.
